tool.name: Polars
tool.tagline: Fast multi-threaded DataFrames with a lazy, optimizing query engine
tool.description: Polars is a DataFrame library written in Rust with a Python API, built on the Apache Arrow memory format. Its expression API and lazy query engine let it optimize whole queries, use every CPU core and process data larger than memory with streaming. Learn it when pandas becomes too slow or too memory-hungry, or when you want cleaner, SQL-like data pipelines in Python.

glossary.def: A table of data in code: named columns of equal length, where every value in a column has the same type. The main object in Polars and pandas.
One named column of a DataFrame: a list of values that all share one data type.
In Polars, a description of how to compute a column, like pl.col("price") * 1.2. It does nothing on its own; a context such as select or filter runs it.
In Polars, a DataFrame method that runs expressions: select, with_columns, filter, or group_by().agg().
A standard way of laying out table data in memory, column by column, shared by many tools so they can pass data between each other without converting it.
Splitting rows into groups that share a value (such as the same shop) and computing a summary, like a total or count, for each group.
A Polars table that hasn't been computed yet: a plan of steps that runs only when you call .collect(), so Polars can optimise the whole plan first.
The part of Polars that runs a lazy query in small pieces of rows at a time, on all cores, so the data never has to fit in memory all at once.
Combining two tables by matching rows that share a key value, such as attaching each order to its customer by customer id.
In Polars, a way to pick many columns at once by type or name pattern, e.g. cs.numeric() for every number column.
A placeholder like %Y (4-digit year), %m (month) or %d (day) in a pattern that describes how a date is written as text, e.g. "%d/%m/%Y" for 24/12/2026.

Polars text types for columns with few distinct values repeated many times (like country names): each value is stored once and rows hold small numbers pointing to it. Enum fixes the allowed values up front.
A calculation done within groups of rows (such as each region) that still returns a value for every row, like each sale's share of its region's total.
Reshaping a table from long to wide: the distinct values of one column (such as months) become new column names.
Reshaping a table from wide to long: several columns (such as jan, feb, mar) are turned into rows with one column for the name and one for the value.
A query optimisation: reading only the columns a query actually uses, straight from the file, instead of loading every column and dropping most later.
A query optimisation: applying a filter as early as possible, ideally while reading the file, so rows that can't match are never loaded.
A block of rows inside a Parquet file, stored with small statistics such as each column's minimum and maximum, so a reader can skip whole blocks that can't match a filter.
User-defined function: your own function handed to a data tool to run on its data, as opposed to one of the tool's built-in operations.
A Polars column type where each row holds a list of values of any length, such as the tags of a post.
A Polars column type where each row holds several named fields, like a small row inside one cell, e.g. {lat, lon}.
A join that matches each row to the nearest row in the other table by a sorted key, usually time, instead of an exact match: e.g. the last price recorded at or before each sale.
A calculation over the last stretch of rows or time before each row, such as the average of the past 7 days, recomputed as it slides along.
In Polars, the end of a lazy query that writes results straight to a file as they are produced, instead of collecting them into memory first.
Storing a large data set as files in folders named after column values, like year=2026/month=03/, so a reader can skip whole folders that a filter rules out.
Your own Polars expression written in Rust and compiled, so it runs inside the engine at full speed on all cores, like a built-in.
In Polars, one piece of a column's memory. A column can consist of several chunks (e.g. after stacking tables); rechunk() merges them into one continuous block.
Sharing data between two parts of a program, or two libraries, by pointing at the same memory instead of copying it, so it costs almost nothing however big the data is.

concepts.name: DataFrame, Series and schema
concepts.summary: Create a Polars DataFrame, read its schema, and look at the data with head, describe and glimpse.
concepts.why: Everything in Polars starts with a DataFrame of named, typed columns, so you need to read its size and schema at a glance.
concepts.body:
A lot of real-world data is a table: a spreadsheet of orders, a list of customers. Each **row** is one record (one order). Each **column** is one kind of value across all rows (the price of every order). Polars is a third-party library for working with such tables quickly, even with millions of rows. Import it as `import polars as pl`, the universal convention.

A Polars table is a **DataFrame**. Each of its columns is a **Series**: a named list of values that all have the same data type, such as `Int64` (whole numbers), `Float64` (decimals), `String` (text), `Boolean` or `Date`. The list of column names with their types is the table's **schema**.

The quickest way to build one is from a dict of lists, one list per column: `pl.DataFrame({"name": [...], "age": [...]})`. Polars works out each column's type, or you choose with `schema_overrides={"age": pl.Int32}`. A `None` in a list becomes **null**, Polars' marker for a missing value.

Things to know straight away:

- `df.shape` gives (rows, columns), also `df.height` and `df.width`; `df.columns` the names; `df.schema` the names with types.
- `df.head(n)`, `df.tail(n)` and `df.sample(n)` show some rows; `df.glimpse()` shows one line per column, handy for wide tables.
- `df.describe()` gives, per column, the count, number of nulls, average, smallest, largest and a few in-between values.
- `df["age"]` gives one column as a Series; `df.to_dicts()` and `df.rows()` give plain Python data.

Unlike pandas, another popular table library, Polars has **no index**: no extra row labels. You find rows by their position or by the values in their columns.

Polars also never changes a DataFrame in place. Methods return a new DataFrame. Columns that didn't change are shared with the old one rather than copied, so this is cheap.

Internally, columns are stored in the **Apache Arrow** layout, a standard way of laying out table data that many tools share.
concepts.code:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "name": ["Ana", "Ben", "Cy"],
        "age": [34, 28, None],
        "city": ["Oslo", "Lima", "Oslo"],
    },
    schema_overrides={"age": pl.Int32},
)
print(df.shape)                 # (3, 3)
print(df.schema)
# Schema({'name': String, 'age': Int32, 'city': String})
print(df["age"].null_count())   # 1
print(df.head(2).rows())        # [('Ana', 34, 'Oslo'), ('Ben', 28, 'Lima')]
print(df.to_dicts()[2])         # {'name': 'Cy', 'age': None, 'city': 'Oslo'}
takeaways: A DataFrame is a set of named, typed Series of equal length
Check `df.schema` early: types decide what you can do with a column
There is no index; rows are found by their values or positions
pitfalls: Expecting pandas habits such as `df.loc` or an index: Polars has neither.

quiz.q: Which statement about a Polars DataFrame is true?
options: Every column has one data type, and there are no extra row labels (no index)
One column can freely mix numbers and text
Methods like with_columns change the DataFrame in place
Columns have no names, only positions
quiz.explain: Each column is a Series with a single type, and Polars has no row index.

concepts.name: Expressions and contexts
concepts.summary: Describe column calculations with pl.col expressions and run them in select, with_columns and filter.
concepts.why: Almost every Polars operation is written as an expression, and expressions are what make Polars fast.
concepts.body:
In Polars you rarely loop over rows. Instead you describe what to compute for a whole column, and Polars does it. That description is an **expression**: `pl.col("price") * 1.2` means "the price column times 1.2". It is not a result yet, just a recipe.

Nothing runs until you hand the expression to a **context**, a DataFrame method that carries out expressions:

- `df.select(...)` returns only the columns you compute.
- `df.with_columns(...)` returns all existing columns plus new or replaced ones.
- `df.filter(...)` keeps the rows where a True/False expression is True.
- `df.group_by(...).agg(...)` computes per group (a later lesson).

Build expressions from `pl.col("name")`, fixed values `pl.lit(5)` (the same value for every row), and operators (`+`, `*`, `>`, `&`, `|`, `~`). Methods chain on: `pl.col("x").round(1)`, `pl.col("x").cast(pl.Float32)` to change the type, and `pl.col("name").str.to_uppercase()`, where `.str` holds the text methods. Name the output with `.alias("new")`, or use keyword arguments: `with_columns(total=pl.col("a") + pl.col("b"))`.

Expressions inside one context are **independent** of each other. So Polars works on them at the same time, each on its own **CPU core** (a modern computer has several cores, each able to run work on its own). The flip side: a column created in a `with_columns` call can't be used by other expressions in that same call. Chain a second `with_columns` if one new column depends on another.

Because an expression is just a value, you can store it in a variable or return it from a function, and reuse it in many places. That keeps long chains of steps short and readable.
concepts.code:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"item": ["tea", "cake", "jam"],
                   "price": [3.0, 4.5, 2.0], "qty": [2, 1, 5]})

revenue = pl.col("price") * pl.col("qty")      # a reusable recipe

out = (
    df.with_columns(revenue.alias("revenue"),
                    item=pl.col("item").str.to_uppercase())
      .with_columns(big=pl.col("revenue") > 5)  # needs the column above
      .filter(pl.col("qty") > 1)
      .select("item", "revenue", "big")
)
print(out.rows())   # [('TEA', 6.0, True), ('JAM', 10.0, True)]
takeaways: An expression describes a calculation; a context runs it
`select` keeps only computed columns, `with_columns` adds to the table
Expressions in one context run side by side and can't see each other's outputs
pitfalls: Referring to a column created earlier in the same `with_columns` call: it doesn't exist yet.

quiz.q: df.with_columns(a2=pl.col('a') * 2, a4=pl.col('a2') * 2) fails. Why?
options: a2 doesn't exist yet inside the same call; chain another with_columns
quiz.explain: Expressions in one context all work on the input table, which has no a2 column yet.

concepts.name: Reading and writing CSV and Parquet
concepts.summary: Load files with read_csv and read_parquet, fix column types on the way in, and save results as Parquet.
concepts.why: Getting data in with the right types, and saving it in a fast, typed format, is the first step of every real job.
concepts.body:
Polars reads files into DataFrames with functions such as `pl.read_csv`, `pl.read_parquet`, `pl.read_json`, `pl.read_ndjson` (one JSON record per line) and `pl.read_excel`. These read the whole file straight away. Writers mirror them: `df.write_csv`, `df.write_parquet`, `df.write_json`.

Useful `read_csv` options:

- `separator=";"`, `has_header=False`
- `columns=["a", "b"]` to read only some columns
- `schema_overrides={"zip": pl.String}` to stop codes with leading zeros, like 02134, becoming numbers
- `try_parse_dates=True` to turn text like `2026-03-01` into a `Date`
- `null_values=["", "NA", "-"]` for extra markers that mean "missing"

In Polars 2, `read_csv` runs on the same engine as the `scan_*` functions you'll meet later, so it reads with several of your computer's cores at once. It also accepts a list of files, or a pattern such as `"data/*.csv"`, meaning every CSV file in the data folder.

**Parquet** is the file type to prefer for data you keep. It stores the data column by column, shrunk with **compression** (like a zip file), together with the schema. So reading is fast and exact, with no type guessing, and `pl.read_parquet(path, columns=[...])` reads only the columns you ask for. If you will reread a CSV file often, convert it to Parquet once.

For files bigger than your computer's memory, or when you need only part of a file, use the `scan_*` functions instead; they come up in a later lesson.
concepts.code:
import polars as pl

with open("orders.csv", "w") as f:
    f.write("id;day;zip;qty\n1;2026-03-01;02134;2\n2;2026-03-02;10001;NA\n")

df = pl.read_csv(
    "orders.csv",
    separator=";",
    schema_overrides={"zip": pl.String},   # keep the leading zero
    null_values=["NA"],
    try_parse_dates=True,
)
print(df.schema)
# Schema({'id': Int64, 'day': Date, 'zip': String, 'qty': Int64})

df.write_parquet("orders.parquet")
back = pl.read_parquet("orders.parquet", columns=["zip", "qty"])
print(back.rows())   # [('02134', 2), ('10001', None)]
takeaways: `schema_overrides`, `null_values` and `try_parse_dates` fix most CSV type problems
Parquet keeps the schema exactly and reads only the columns you ask for
`read_*` loads the whole file at once; `scan_*` is for big or partial reads
pitfalls: Letting ID or postal-code columns be read as numbers and losing their leading zeros.

quiz.q: Why is Parquet usually better than CSV for data you load again and again?
options: You can read it in a text editor
It stores the column types and compressed columns, so loading is fast and exact
It can only hold one column
quiz.explain: Parquet keeps the schema and stores columns separately, so there is no type guessing and you can read just some columns.

concepts.name: Filtering, sorting and selecting rows
concepts.summary: Keep rows with filter, combine conditions with & and |, and order rows with sort, head and top_k.
concepts.why: Most questions about data start with 'which rows' and 'in what order'.
concepts.body:
`df.filter(expr)` keeps the rows where a True/False expression is True. Combine conditions with `&` (and), `|` (or) and `~` (not), and wrap each comparison in parentheses, because Python works out `&` before comparisons like `>`. Passing several expressions, `df.filter(cond1, cond2)`, means all of them must hold.

Where the condition is null, for example because the age is missing, the row is dropped: Polars can't say it matches, so it isn't kept.

Handy conditions:

- `pl.col("city").is_in(["Oslo", "Lima"])`
- `pl.col("age").is_between(18, 65)` (both ends included by default)
- `pl.col("name").str.starts_with("A")`
- `pl.col("x").is_null()` / `.is_not_null()`

Sorting: `df.sort("age")`, `df.sort("age", descending=True)`, or by several columns, `df.sort(["city", "age"], descending=[False, True])`. Nulls go first by default; pass `nulls_last=True` to change that. For the n largest values use `df.top_k(3, by="score")` or `df.bottom_k(...)`, which is faster than sorting everything.

Taking rows by position still exists for quick looks: `df.head(5)`, `df.slice(10, 5)` (5 rows starting at row 10), `df[2:4]` (rows 2 and 3). But since Polars has no index, real logic should pick rows by their values, not their positions.

Removing duplicate rows is `df.unique(subset=["email"], keep="first", maintain_order=True)`.
concepts.code:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Ana", "Ben", "Cy", "Di"],
    "age": [34, 17, None, 52],
    "city": ["Oslo", "Lima", "Oslo", "Rome"],
})

adults_oslo_or_rome = df.filter(
    (pl.col("age") >= 18) & pl.col("city").is_in(["Oslo", "Rome"])
)
print(adults_oslo_or_rome["name"].to_list())     # ['Ana', 'Di']  (Cy's null age is dropped)

print(df.sort("age", descending=True, nulls_last=True)["name"].to_list())
# ['Di', 'Ana', 'Ben', 'Cy']
print(df.top_k(2, by="age")["name"].to_list())   # ['Di', 'Ana']
takeaways: Combine conditions with `&`, `|`, `~` and parentheses
Rows whose condition is null are filtered out
`top_k` beats sorting everything and taking the head
pitfalls: Writing `cond1 and cond2`: Python's `and` doesn't work on expressions; use `&`.

quiz.q: Which filter keeps people aged 18 or over who do NOT live in Oslo?
quiz.explain: Use & for and, ~ for not, and parentheses around each comparison.

concepts.name: Conditional columns with when/then
concepts.summary: Build if/else logic for a column with pl.when().then().otherwise(), chaining several branches.
concepts.why: Grades, flags and business rules are everywhere, and when/then writes them for a whole column at once.
concepts.body:
A Python `if` statement decides once, not separately for each row of a column. Polars uses `pl.when(condition).then(value).otherwise(default)` instead, which decides row by row.

Add more branches with extra `.when(...).then(...)` pairs; the first condition that is true wins, checking from top to bottom. If you leave out `.otherwise(...)`, rows that match no branch become null.

```python
pl.when(pl.col("score") >= 90).then(pl.lit("A"))
  .when(pl.col("score") >= 75).then(pl.lit("B"))
  .otherwise(pl.lit("C"))
```

The values in `then` and `otherwise` can be fixed values or other expressions, so you can choose between columns: `pl.when(pl.col("discount").is_not_null()).then(pl.col("discount")).otherwise(pl.col("price"))`. For that "first value that isn't null" pattern, `pl.coalesce("discount", "price")` is shorter.

A string passed to `then("x")` is read as a **column name**, not as text. Wrap text in `pl.lit("x")` when you mean the text itself.

Polars computes every branch for all rows and then picks per row. That sounds wasteful but is fast, because each branch is one whole-column calculation. The result gets a type that fits all branches, so mixing whole numbers and decimals gives decimals.
concepts.code:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"name": ["Ana", "Ben", "Cy", "Di"],
                   "score": [95, 80, 60, None]})

graded = df.with_columns(
    grade=pl.when(pl.col("score") >= 90).then(pl.lit("A"))
            .when(pl.col("score") >= 75).then(pl.lit("B"))
            .when(pl.col("score").is_not_null()).then(pl.lit("C"))
            # no otherwise: rows matching nothing become null
)
print(graded["grade"].to_list())   # ['A', 'B', 'C', None]

bonus = pl.when(pl.col("grade") == "A").then(10).otherwise(0)
print(graded.select(bonus.alias("bonus"))["bonus"].to_list())   # [10, 0, 0, 0]
takeaways: `pl.when(...).then(...).otherwise(...)` is if/elif/else for a whole column
The first true branch wins; no otherwise means null
Wrap text values in `pl.lit()`; bare strings are column names
pitfalls: Writing `then("A")` when you meant the text A: Polars looks for a column called A.

quiz.q: What does pl.when(pl.col('x') > 0).then(pl.lit('pos')) give for a row where x is -3?
quiz.explain: Without otherwise, rows matching no branch get null.

concepts.name: Group by and aggregate
concepts.summary: Summarise data per group with group_by().agg(), computing several totals, counts or averages at once.
concepts.why: Totals, counts and averages per group are the most common analysis there is.
concepts.body:
"Total sales per shop" means: split the rows into groups that share a shop, then boil each group down to one number. Boiling many values down to one, like a sum or an average, is called **aggregation**. In Polars, `df.group_by("shop").agg(...)` splits the rows by the key column, works out each expression inside every group, and returns one row per group. Group by several columns with `group_by("a", "b")`.

Inside `agg`, any expression works:

- `pl.col("amount").sum()`, `.mean()` (average), `.median()`, `.min()`, `.max()`, `.std()` (spread)
- `pl.len()` for the number of rows, `pl.col("user").n_unique()` for the number of different values
- `pl.col("amount").filter(pl.col("type") == "refund").sum()` to sum only some rows
- `pl.col("item").first()`, or `pl.col("item")` alone, which collects each group's values into a **list**

Name results with `.alias()` or keyword arguments, e.g. `agg(total=pl.col("amount").sum())`. All expressions in one `agg` run side by side on different CPU cores.

**The order of groups is not guaranteed.** Groups come back in whatever order the cores finish them, so don't rely on the order in which keys first appeared. Sort the result, or pass `maintain_order=True` (slower) when order matters.

The group keys are ordinary columns in the result, ready for the next step. If you know SQL, the database language, `group_by().agg()` is its `GROUP BY` with the selected values inside `agg`.
concepts.code:
import polars as pl

sales = pl.DataFrame({
    "shop": ["A", "B", "A", "B", "A"],
    "kind": ["sale", "sale", "refund", "sale", "sale"],
    "amount": [10.0, 5.0, -3.0, 7.0, 4.0],
})

summary = (
    sales.group_by("shop")
    .agg(
        n=pl.len(),
        net=pl.col("amount").sum(),
        refunds=pl.col("amount").filter(pl.col("kind") == "refund").sum(),
        kinds=pl.col("kind").unique().sort(),
    )
    .sort("shop")                      # output order is not guaranteed
)
print(summary.rows())
# [('A', 3, 11.0, -3.0, ['refund', 'sale']), ('B', 2, 12.0, 0.0, ['sale'])]
takeaways: `group_by(keys).agg(exprs)` gives one row per group
Any expression can be an aggregation, including filtered ones
Sort the result or use `maintain_order=True`; group order is not guaranteed
pitfalls: Assuming groups come back in first-appearance order.

quiz.q: What type is the column produced by df.group_by('k').agg(pl.col('v')), with no sum or other summary applied?
quiz.explain: A column given to agg without a summary collects each group's values into a list.

concepts.name: Missing data: null and NaN
concepts.summary: Tell null and NaN apart in Polars and handle gaps with is_null, fill_null, drop_nulls and coalesce.
concepts.why: Real data has gaps, and mixing up null and NaN gives silently wrong counts and averages.
concepts.body:
Polars has one marker for a missing value in every type: **null**. It works the same in number, text, date and True/False columns, so a whole-number column with a gap stays a whole-number column.

**NaN** ("not a number") is different. It is a real decimal value, the result of undefined maths such as `0.0 / 0.0`. Polars does not treat NaN as missing: `is_null()` is False for NaN, `null_count()` doesn't count it, and the `mean()` of a column containing NaN is NaN. Use `is_nan()` and `fill_nan()` for those values, or turn them into nulls with `fill_nan(None)`.

Tools for nulls:

- `pl.col("x").is_null()`, `.is_not_null()`, `df.null_count()`
- `pl.col("x").fill_null(0)`, or `.fill_null(strategy="forward")` to repeat the last known value, or `"mean"` for the average
- `df.drop_nulls()` or `df.drop_nulls(subset=["x"])` to remove rows with gaps
- `pl.coalesce("a", "b", pl.lit(0))` takes the first value that isn't null

Sums, averages, minimums and other summaries skip nulls. `count()` counts only values that aren't null, while `pl.len()` counts rows. Comparing anything with null gives null, which `filter` treats as "don't keep".

When you convert a pandas table, `pl.from_pandas(pdf, nan_to_null=True)` (the default) turns its NaN gaps into proper nulls.
concepts.code:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"x": [1.0, None, float("nan"), 4.0]})

print(df.select(
    nulls=pl.col("x").null_count(),
    nans=pl.col("x").is_nan().sum(),
    count=pl.col("x").count(),        # non-null values, NaN included
    rows=pl.len(),
).row(0))                             # (1, 1, 3, 4)

print(df["x"].mean())                 # nan  (NaN poisons the mean)
clean = df.with_columns(pl.col("x").fill_nan(None))
print(clean["x"].mean())              # 2.5  (nulls are skipped)
print(clean["x"].fill_null(strategy="forward").to_list())
# [1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 4.0]
takeaways: null marks a missing value in any type; NaN is a decimal value
Aggregations skip nulls but not NaN
`count()` counts values that aren't null; `pl.len()` counts rows
pitfalls: Using `is_null()` to find NaN values in decimal columns: it returns False for NaN.

quiz.q: A Float64 column holds [2.0, NaN, null]. What is its null_count()?
quiz.explain: Only the null is missing; NaN is an ordinary decimal value to Polars.

concepts.name: The lazy API: scan and collect
concepts.summary: Build a LazyFrame with scan_* or .lazy(), chain steps into a query plan, and run it with collect().
concepts.why: Lazy mode is where Polars gets its biggest speed and memory wins, and it is the recommended way to write multi-step data jobs.
concepts.body:
So far every method ran immediately and returned a result. That is **eager** mode. In **lazy** mode, methods only record what you want, building a **query plan**: the list of steps for your **query** (the question you are asking of the data). Nothing happens until you call `.collect()`. The lazy version of a DataFrame is a **LazyFrame**. Get one from `pl.scan_parquet(...)`, `pl.scan_csv(...)`, `pl.scan_ndjson(...)` or `df.lazy()`.

Why wait? Because Polars sees the whole question before doing any work, it can plan it well. It reads only the columns you use, skips parts of a Parquet file that can't match your filter, applies filters while reading instead of after, drops calculations nobody uses, and runs steps on several cores at once. Your code reads the same as eager code; only the start (`scan_*` or `.lazy()`) and the `collect()` at the end differ.

```python
q = (pl.scan_parquet("events/*.parquet")
       .filter(pl.col("country") == "NO")
       .group_by("day").agg(pl.len()))
df = q.collect()
```

In Polars 2, `collect()` uses the **streaming engine** by default. It works through the data in small pieces of rows on all cores, so the input can be bigger than your computer's memory (RAM). One consequence: row order after joins, group-bys and unpivots is not guaranteed, so sort explicitly when order matters. `collect(engine="in-memory")` picks the older engine that loads everything at once.

`lf.collect_schema()` tells you the result's columns and types without running anything, and `lf.head(5).collect()` is the quick way to peek. Mixing modes is fine: collect, do something eager, then `.lazy()` again.
concepts.code:
import polars as pl

pl.DataFrame({
    "day": ["mon", "mon", "tue", "tue", "tue"],
    "country": ["NO", "SE", "NO", "NO", "SE"],
    "ms": [120, 80, 95, 130, 70],
}).write_parquet("events.parquet")

q = (
    pl.scan_parquet("events.parquet")          # nothing is read yet
    .filter(pl.col("country") == "NO")
    .group_by("day")
    .agg(n=pl.len(), avg_ms=pl.col("ms").mean())
    .sort("day")
)
print(type(q).__name__)          # LazyFrame
print(q.collect_schema())        # Schema({'day': String, 'n': UInt32, 'avg_ms': Float64})
print(q.collect().rows())        # [('mon', 1, 120.0), ('tue', 2, 112.5)]
takeaways: A LazyFrame builds a plan; `collect()` runs it
Start from `scan_*` so Polars can skip unneeded columns and rows while reading
Polars 2 collects with the streaming engine by default; sort if order matters
pitfalls: Calling `collect()` after every step, which throws away most of the planning benefit.

quiz.q: Why does pl.scan_parquet(...).select('a').collect() usually read less data than pl.read_parquet(...).select('a')?
options: The lazy plan passes the column choice to the file reader, so only column a is read
select is ignored in eager mode
quiz.explain: Seeing the whole plan, the scan reads only the columns the query uses; the eager call reads them all first.

concepts.name: Joins and concatenation
concepts.summary: Combine tables with join (inner, left, full, semi, anti) and stack them with pl.concat.
concepts.why: Real analyses pull together several tables, and the join type decides which rows survive.
concepts.body:
Data is often split across tables: users in one, orders in another, linked by a user id. A **join** combines them by matching rows that share a value in a **key** column. `left.join(right, on="key", how=...)` does it. Use `left_on=`/`right_on=` when the key has different names, and a list when the key is several columns together.

The `how` argument decides which rows survive:

- `"inner"` (default): only keys found in both tables.
- `"left"`: every left row, with nulls where the right has no match. `"right"` is the mirror image.
- `"full"`: everything from both; pass `coalesce=True` to merge the two key columns into one.
- `"semi"`: left rows that have a match, without adding any right columns.
- `"anti"`: left rows with *no* match, perfect for "customers who never ordered".
- `"cross"`: every combination of a left row and a right row.

Other columns with the same name on both sides get a `_right` suffix (change it with `suffix=`). Null keys don't match each other unless you pass `nulls_equal=True`.

A key that repeats multiplies rows: a user with 3 orders appears 3 times. Guard against surprises with `validate="m:1"` (many-to-one; also `"1:1"`, `"1:m"`), which raises an error if the right side's keys aren't unique. It's a cheap check that catches many bugs.

Join output order is not guaranteed by default; pass `maintain_order="left"` or sort afterwards.

To stack tables on top of each other, use `pl.concat([a, b])` when they have the same columns, or `how="diagonal"` when they differ, filling gaps with null. `how="horizontal"` puts tables side by side and, in Polars 2, requires the same number of rows.
concepts.code:
import polars as pl

users = pl.DataFrame({"uid": [1, 2, 3], "name": ["Ana", "Ben", "Cy"]})
orders = pl.DataFrame({"uid": [1, 1, 3, 4], "total": [10, 5, 7, 9]})

left = users.join(orders, on="uid", how="left", maintain_order="left")
print(left.rows())
# [(1, 'Ana', 10), (1, 'Ana', 5), (2, 'Ben', None), (3, 'Cy', 7)]

never = users.join(orders, on="uid", how="anti")
print(never["name"].to_list())        # ['Ben']

try:
    orders.join(users, on="uid", how="left", validate="1:1")
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)           # ComputeError (uid repeats in orders)

stacked = pl.concat([users, pl.DataFrame({"uid": [9]})], how="diagonal")
print(stacked.tail(1).rows())         # [(9, None)]
takeaways: Pick the join type by which rows must survive: inner, left, full, semi, anti
`validate="m:1"` catches unexpected duplicate keys
`pl.concat(how="diagonal")` stacks tables with different columns
pitfalls: Joining on a key that repeats on both sides and silently multiplying rows.

quiz.q: You want customers that have at least one order, with only the customer columns. Which join?
quiz.explain: A semi join keeps left rows that have a match and adds no right-side columns or duplicate rows.

concepts.name: Selecting many columns: selectors
concepts.summary: Apply one expression to many columns with pl.all, lists of names, type-based picks and selectors.
concepts.why: Wide tables need the same step on many columns without writing one line per column.
concepts.body:
One expression can stand for many columns. `pl.col("a", "b").round(1)` rounds both; `pl.col(pl.Float64)` picks every `Float64` column; `pl.all()` picks every column, and `pl.all().exclude("id")` all but some.

You can also pick names by pattern with a **regular expression**, a mini-language for describing text: `pl.col("^sales_.*$")` means "names that start with sales_". Polars only treats the name as a pattern when it starts with `^` and ends with `$`.

The **selectors** module, imported as `import polars.selectors as cs`, is more flexible:

- `cs.numeric()`, `cs.string()`, `cs.temporal()` (dates and times), `cs.boolean()`
- `cs.starts_with("sales_")`, `cs.ends_with("_id")`, `cs.contains("price")`, `cs.matches(pattern)`
- `cs.by_name("a", "b")`, `cs.first()`, `cs.last()`
- combine them like sets: `|` (in either), `&` (in both), `-` (in the first but not the second), `~` (everything else)

The expanded results keep their original names, so in `with_columns` they replace the input columns. To keep both, rename with the methods grouped under `.name`: `.name.suffix("_z")`, `.name.prefix(...)`, `.name.map(func)`.

In Polars 2, combining a selector with `pl.col(...)` using `&`, `|` or `^` does True/False logic on the column values, not column picking. Stay with selectors, using `cs.by_name(...)`, when you mean "these columns and those".

`cs.expand_selector(df, selector)` shows which columns a selector picks, handy when it isn't doing what you expect.
concepts.code:
import polars as pl
import polars.selectors as cs

df = pl.DataFrame({
    "id": [1, 2], "name": ["a", "b"],
    "sales_q1": [10.0, 20.0], "sales_q2": [30.0, 10.0], "rate": [0.5, 0.25],
})

print(cs.expand_selector(df, cs.numeric() - cs.by_name("id")))
# ('sales_q1', 'sales_q2', 'rate')

out = df.with_columns(
    (cs.starts_with("sales_") / 10).name.suffix("_k"),
    pl.col(pl.String).str.to_uppercase(),
)
print(out.columns)
# ['id', 'name', 'sales_q1', 'sales_q2', 'rate', 'sales_q1_k', 'sales_q2_k']
print(out.select(pl.sum_horizontal(cs.ends_with("_k"))).to_series().to_list())
# [4.0, 3.0]
takeaways: `pl.col(dtype)`, `pl.all()` and `^...$` patterns expand into many columns
Selectors combine like sets with `|`, `&`, `-`, `~`
Use `.name.suffix()` to keep the originals when transforming many columns
pitfalls: Forgetting `^...$` around a pattern in `pl.col`, so it is read as a plain column name.

quiz.q: What does df.with_columns(cs.numeric() * 2) do to the numeric columns?
options: Replaces them in place, keeping their names
quiz.explain: Expanded expressions keep their input names, so with_columns overwrites the originals.

concepts.name: Strings, dates and casting
concepts.summary: Use the str and dt method groups, turn text into dates with str.to_date, and convert types with cast.
concepts.why: Text and dates arrive messy in almost all real data; cleaning them a whole column at a time is a daily task.
concepts.body:
Methods for one kind of column live in groups on expressions: `.str` for text, `.dt` for dates and times. Polars calls these groups namespaces.

The `str` group: `len_chars()`, `to_lowercase()`, `strip_chars()` (remove spaces at the ends), `contains(pattern)`, `replace(pattern, value)` (first match only) and `replace_all`, `extract(pattern, group)`, `split(",")` (gives a list per row), `slice(offset, length)`, `starts_with()`. Patterns are regular expressions (text patterns such as `\d+`, "one or more digits") unless you pass `literal=True`.

Turning text into dates also uses `str`: `str.to_date("%d/%m/%Y")`, `str.to_datetime(...)`, `str.to_time(...)`. The pattern is made of **format codes**: `%d` day, `%m` month, `%Y` four-digit year, so `"%d/%m/%Y"` reads 24/12/2026. In Polars 2, `cast(pl.Date)` on a text column raises an error, so always convert with `str.to_date` and friends. `strict=False` turns text that doesn't fit into null instead of failing.

The `dt` group works on `Date`, `Datetime` (date plus time) and `Duration` (a length of time): `year()`, `month()`, `weekday()` (Monday = 1), `truncate("1mo")` (round down to the month), `offset_by("2d")` (add two days), `strftime(fmt)` (back to text), `total_days()`. `convert_time_zone()` and `replace_time_zone()` handle time zones. Subtracting two dates gives a `Duration`.

Other conversions use `cast`: `pl.col("x").cast(pl.Int32)`. A failing cast raises by default; `cast(..., strict=False)` gives null instead.

To save memory, use smaller number types, and for text columns with a few values repeated many times (countries, statuses) use `pl.Categorical` or `pl.Enum`. They store each distinct text once and keep a small number per row; `Enum` also fixes the list of allowed values up front.
concepts.code:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({
    "raw": ["  Oslo-2026/03/01 ", "lima-2026/12/24", "rome-bad"],
    "qty": ["3", "x", "5"],
})

out = df.select(
    city=pl.col("raw").str.strip_chars().str.extract(r"^(\w+)-", 1)
            .str.to_titlecase(),
    day=pl.col("raw").str.extract(r"(\d{4}/\d{2}/\d{2})", 1)
           .str.to_date("%Y/%m/%d", strict=False),
    qty=pl.col("qty").cast(pl.Int64, strict=False),
).with_columns(
    month=pl.col("day").dt.month(),
    weekday=pl.col("day").dt.weekday(),
)
print(out.rows())
# [('Oslo', datetime.date(2026, 3, 1), 3, 3, 7),
#  ('Lima', datetime.date(2026, 12, 24), None, 12, 4),
#  ('Rome', None, 5, None, None)]
takeaways: `.str` and `.dt` hold text and date methods that work on whole columns
Convert text with `str.to_date`/`to_datetime` and format codes; Polars 2 won't cast text to dates
`strict=False` turns bad values into null instead of raising
pitfalls: Expecting `str.replace` to replace every match: it replaces the first; use `replace_all`.

quiz.q: In Polars 2, how should you turn a text column like '2026-03-01' into a Date?
quiz.explain: Casting text to dates now raises; parse with str.to_date (or to_datetime) and a format pattern instead.

concepts.name: Window functions with over()
concepts.summary: Compute per-group values without collapsing rows using .over(): group totals, shares, ranks and running totals.
concepts.why: Questions like 'share of the group total' or 'rank within category' need group results next to each row.
concepts.body:
`group_by().agg()` gives one row per group. Often you want the group's result next to every original row instead: each sale beside its region's total. That's a **window function**, and in Polars you write it as `expr.over("group")`. The expression is worked out within each group, but every row keeps its place, so it fits in `with_columns` or `select` next to ordinary columns.

- Group total on every row: `pl.col("sales").sum().over("region")`.
- Share of the group: `pl.col("sales") / pl.col("sales").sum().over("region")`.
- Rank within the group: `pl.col("sales").rank("dense", descending=True).over("region")` (`"dense"` gives ties the same rank with no gaps).
- Running total: `pl.col("sales").cum_sum().over("region", order_by="day")`.
- Previous row's value: `pl.col("price").shift(1).over("ticker", order_by="ts")`.

Several group columns work too: `.over("region", "year")`. The `order_by=` argument sorts within each group just for that calculation, so you don't have to sort the whole table first.

`mapping_strategy` controls how results are put back. The default, `"group_to_rows"`, puts each result on its original row. `"explode"` is faster but reorders the rows group by group. `"join"` puts the whole group's results, as a list, on each row.

Filtering on a window value is a classic pattern. Keep the top two rows per region with `df.filter(pl.col("sales").rank("ordinal", descending=True).over("region") <= 2)`. If you know SQL, `.over()` is its `OVER (PARTITION BY ...)`.
concepts.code:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({
    "region": ["N", "N", "N", "S", "S"],
    "day": [3, 1, 2, 1, 2],
    "sales": [30, 10, 20, 5, 15],
})

out = df.with_columns(
    share=(pl.col("sales") / pl.col("sales").sum().over("region")).round(2),
    rank=pl.col("sales").rank("dense", descending=True).over("region"),
    running=pl.col("sales").cum_sum().over("region", order_by="day"),
)
print(out.rows())
# [('N', 3, 30, 0.5, 1, 60), ('N', 1, 10, 0.17, 3, 10), ('N', 2, 20, 0.33, 2, 30),
#  ('S', 1, 5, 0.25, 2, 5), ('S', 2, 15, 0.75, 1, 20)]
takeaways: `.over(keys)` computes per group but returns one value per row
Use `order_by=` for running totals and previous values within groups
Filter on a rank inside `.over()` for the top n per group
pitfalls: Using group_by and then a join to put group totals on each row, when one `.over()` does it.

quiz.q: df has 10 rows in 3 regions. How many rows does df.select(pl.col('x').mean().over('region')) return?
quiz.explain: over() keeps every row and places each region's mean on the rows of that region.

concepts.name: Reshaping: pivot and unpivot
concepts.summary: Turn long data wide with pivot and wide data long with unpivot, and know which shape each task wants.
concepts.why: Reports want wide tables while grouping and charts want long ones, so you'll convert back and forth constantly.
concepts.body:
The same numbers can be laid out in two shapes. **Long** data has one row per measurement: `(store, month, sales)`. **Wide** data spreads one kind of value across several columns: `store, jan, feb, mar`.

To **pivot** is to go from long to wide: `df.pivot(on="month", index="store", values="sales", aggregate_function="sum")`. Each distinct value of the `on` column becomes a new column, and each `index` value becomes one row. If several rows share the same `index` and `on` pair, `aggregate_function` says how to combine them (`"sum"`, `"mean"`, `"first"`, `"len"`, or an expression). Combinations with no rows become null, except with `"sum"` or `"len"`, where they become 0.

Pivot only works on an eager DataFrame, not in a lazy plan: a plan must know its result's columns in advance, and pivot's columns come from the data. In a lazy query, use group_by with one filtered aggregation per column instead, like `pl.col("sales").filter(pl.col("month") == "jan").sum().alias("jan")`.

To **unpivot** is to go back from wide to long: `df.unpivot(index="store", on=["jan", "feb"], variable_name="month", value_name="sales")`. Leaving out `on` unpivots every column except the index, and selectors work too: `on=cs.numeric()`. This used to be called `melt`, which was removed in Polars 2.

Rule of thumb: keep data long while you compute (group_by, joins and charts are all easier) and pivot only at the end, for display.
concepts.code:
import polars as pl

long = pl.DataFrame({
    "store": ["A", "A", "A", "B"],
    "month": ["jan", "feb", "feb", "jan"],
    "sales": [10, 4, 6, 7],
})

wide = long.pivot(on="month", index="store", values="sales",
                  aggregate_function="sum").sort("store")
print(wide.rows())      # [('A', 10, 10), ('B', 7, 0)]  (sum of nothing is 0)
print(wide.columns)     # ['store', 'jan', 'feb']

back = wide.unpivot(index="store", variable_name="month",
                    value_name="sales").sort("store", "month")
print(back.rows())
# [('A', 'feb', 10), ('A', 'jan', 10), ('B', 'feb', 0), ('B', 'jan', 7)]
takeaways: `pivot` turns long into wide; `unpivot` turns wide into long (formerly `melt`)
Pass `aggregate_function` when index/on pairs repeat
Compute in long form, pivot at the end for display
pitfalls: Pivoting a column with thousands of distinct values and getting a table with thousands of columns.

quiz.q: Why can't pivot be part of a lazy query plan directly?
options: Its result's column names depend on the data, so the plan can't know them in advance
quiz.explain: A lazy plan needs to know its result schema; pivot's columns come from the values in the data.

concepts.name: Query plans and optimizations
concepts.summary: Read a lazy query plan with explain(), and see projection pushdown, predicate pushdown and repeated-work removal at work.
concepts.why: Knowing what the optimiser does lets you write queries it can speed up, and spot why one is slow.
concepts.body:
Before running a lazy query, Polars' optimiser rewrites the query plan into a faster one that gives the same result. `lf.explain()` prints that **optimised** plan as text; `lf.explain(optimized=False)` shows your query as you wrote it. Read the plan from the bottom up: reading the file is at the bottom, the last step at the top. `lf.show_graph()` draws it as a diagram (it needs the graphviz program installed).

The main optimisations:

- **Projection pushdown**: only the columns the query uses are read from the file. In the plan the scan shows something like `PROJECT 2/5 COLUMNS`.
- **Predicate pushdown**: filters move as early as possible, ideally into the scan itself (`SELECTION:` on the scan step). A Parquet file stores its rows in blocks called **row groups**, each with the minimum and maximum of every column, so the reader can skip whole blocks that can't match.
- **Slice pushdown**: `head(n)` stops reading once it has n rows.
- **Simplification**: work that only involves fixed values is done once in advance (`pl.lit(2) * 3` becomes 6), and expressions are swapped for cheaper equivalents.
- **Removing repeated work**: a sub-query or expression used twice is computed once.

Some things block these optimisations. A **UDF** (your own Python function, run with `map_elements` or `map_batches`) is a black box to Polars, so filters can't be moved past it. Collecting halfway through cuts the plan in two. And CSV files have no row groups or statistics, so nothing can be skipped.

When two results share work, collect them together with `pl.collect_all([q1, q2])` so the shared part runs once. Switching optimisations off (`collect(optimizations=...)`) is only useful when you suspect the optimiser itself has a bug.
concepts.code:
import polars as pl

pl.DataFrame({"a": range(6), "b": list("xyxyxy"), "c": [1.0] * 6,
              "d": [0] * 6}).write_parquet("t.parquet")

q = (
    pl.scan_parquet("t.parquet")
    .with_columns(a2=pl.col("a") * 2)
    .filter(pl.col("b") == "x")
    .select("a2", "b")
)
plan = q.explain()
print(plan)
# The filter on b and the column list are pushed into the Parquet scan;
# look for the scan node showing PROJECT 2/4 COLUMNS and a SELECTION.
print(q.collect()["a2"].to_list())   # [0, 4, 8]
takeaways: `explain()` shows the optimised plan; read it bottom-up
Projection and predicate pushdown move work into the file reading
Python UDFs and collecting halfway block optimisations
pitfalls: Putting a `map_elements` early in the query and wondering why filters are not pushed down.

quiz.q: A query reads a 50-column Parquet file but uses only 3 columns. Which optimisation keeps the other 47 unread?
quiz.explain: Projection pushdown limits the file reading to the columns the query uses.

concepts.name: Lists, arrays and structs
concepts.summary: Work with List, Array and Struct columns: the list methods, explode, implode, unnest and struct fields.
concepts.why: JSON data, group results and calculations with several outputs all produce nested columns, and built-in nested methods are far faster than Python loops.
concepts.body:
A cell doesn't have to hold a single value. Polars has three nested column types:

- **List**: a list of any length per row, e.g. a post's tags or the result of `str.split`. Methods live in `.list`: `len()`, `get(0)`, `contains(x)`, `sum()`, `sort()`, `unique()`, `join(",")`, `eval(expr)`.
- **Array**: a list of fixed size in every row (`pl.Array(pl.Float32, 3)`), good for coordinates or other fixed-length number lists; methods in `.arr`.
- **Struct**: named fields per row, like a small row inside one cell. Methods in `.struct`: `field("x")`, `rename_fields`, `with_fields`. `df.unnest("col")` spreads the fields out into ordinary columns, and `pl.struct("a", "b")` packs columns into one.

Moving between shapes: `explode("tags")` gives one row per list element. In Polars 2, a row with an empty list produces no rows at all; pass `empty_as_null=True` for the old behaviour of one row with null. The reverse is `group_by(...).agg(pl.col("tags"))`, or `.implode()` to pack a whole column into one list.

Inside `list.eval`, `pl.element()` stands for each element of the list, so `pl.col("scores").list.eval(pl.element().rank())` runs any expression on every list, using all cores. Prefer that to passing a Python function, which runs one list at a time in Python.

Structs are also how functions return several columns at once: `value_counts()` (each value with how often it occurs), `str.extract_groups()`, and `str.json_decode()`, which turns JSON text into structs whose fields you then pick with `struct.field`.
concepts.code:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({
    "user": ["ana", "ben"],
    "tags": ["py,sql", "rust"],
    "geo": [{"lat": 59.9, "lon": 10.7}, {"lat": -12.0, "lon": -77.0}],
})

out = df.with_columns(pl.col("tags").str.split(","))
print(out.select(n=pl.col("tags").list.len(),
                 has_py=pl.col("tags").list.contains("py")).rows())
# [(2, True), (1, False)]

print(out.explode("tags").select("user", "tags").rows())
# [('ana', 'py'), ('ana', 'sql'), ('ben', 'rust')]

print(out.unnest("geo").columns)          # ['user', 'tags', 'lat', 'lon']
print(df.select(pl.col("geo").struct.field("lat")).to_series().to_list())
# [59.9, -12.0]
takeaways: List = any length, Array = fixed size, Struct = named fields
`explode` and `implode` move between nested and flat rows
`list.eval(pl.element()...)` runs expressions inside each list
pitfalls: Looping over a list column in Python instead of using the `.list` methods or `list.eval`.

quiz.q: What does explode('tags') do to a row whose tags list is empty, in Polars 2 by default?
quiz.explain: Polars 2 changed empty_as_null to False by default, so empty lists produce no rows.

concepts.name: Time series: dynamic groups, rolling and asof
concepts.summary: Bucket rows by time with group_by_dynamic, compute rolling windows over time, and match events with join_asof.
concepts.why: Sensor readings, website logs and prices are all time series, and these three tools cover most of what their analysis needs.
concepts.body:
A **time series** is data recorded over time: a temperature every minute, a price on every sale. Polars has three main tools for it, and all of them need the table sorted by the time column first.

**`group_by_dynamic`** puts rows into time buckets, such as hours or days, and aggregates each bucket:

```python
df.sort("ts").group_by_dynamic("ts", every="1h", group_by="sensor").agg(pl.col("v").mean())
```

`every` sets how often a new bucket starts, and `period` how long each one lasts (by default the same as `every`; make it longer for overlapping buckets). `closed` and `label` decide which bucket a row exactly on the edge falls into, and which time names the bucket. Lengths are written as text: `"30m"`, `"1d"`, `"1w"`, `"1mo"`, `"1q"` (a quarter year).

A **rolling window** looks back from each row instead. `df.rolling("ts", period="2d").agg(...)` computes over the previous 2 days at every row, and `pl.col("v").rolling_mean_by("ts", window_size="2d")` does the same inside `with_columns`. The versions without `_by`, such as `rolling_mean(window_size=3)`, count rows instead of time.

An **as-of join**, `join_asof`, matches each left row to the *nearest* right row by time instead of an exact match. The classic case is "the last known price at or before each sale": `sales.join_asof(prices, on="ts", by="product", strategy="backward", tolerance="5s")`. `strategy` can be `"backward"` (earlier), `"forward"` (later) or `"nearest"`, and `tolerance` sets how far away a match may be.

To fill gaps in time, `df.upsample("ts", every="1d")` inserts rows for the missing days, and `fill_null(strategy="forward")` or `interpolate()` (a straight line between neighbours) fills in their values.
concepts.code:
import polars as pl
from datetime import datetime as dt

trades = pl.DataFrame({
    "ts": [dt(2026, 1, 1, 9, 0, 5), dt(2026, 1, 1, 9, 0, 40), dt(2026, 1, 1, 10, 30)],
    "qty": [100, 50, 70],
})
quotes = pl.DataFrame({
    "ts": [dt(2026, 1, 1, 9, 0, 0), dt(2026, 1, 1, 9, 0, 30)],
    "bid": [10.0, 10.5],
})

hourly = trades.group_by_dynamic("ts", every="1h").agg(qty=pl.col("qty").sum())
print(hourly.rows())
# [(datetime(2026, 1, 1, 9, 0), 150), (datetime(2026, 1, 1, 10, 0), 70)]

matched = trades.join_asof(quotes, on="ts", strategy="backward", tolerance="1m")
print(matched["bid"].to_list())   # [10.0, 10.5, None]  (last trade: quote too old)
takeaways: `group_by_dynamic` = fixed time buckets; `rolling` = look-back windows from each row
`join_asof` matches the nearest earlier (or later) row by time
Sort by the time column first; these operations require it
pitfalls: Running `group_by_dynamic` or `join_asof` on unsorted timestamps.

quiz.q: For each trade you need the most recent price quote at or before the trade's time. Which tool?
quiz.explain: An as-of join with strategy 'backward' matches the last right row whose time is at or before the left row's time.

concepts.name: Running SQL on DataFrames
concepts.summary: Query DataFrames and LazyFrames with SQL through pl.sql, SQLContext and LazyFrame.sql.
concepts.why: SQL lets analysts and existing queries use Polars directly, and mixing SQL with expressions is often the clearest code.
concepts.body:
**SQL** is the standard language for asking questions of tables, used by almost every database: `SELECT country, SUM(total) FROM orders GROUP BY country`. Many people know it, and a lot of existing code is written in it. Polars includes a SQL engine that translates SQL into the same lazy query plans as expressions, so it gets the same optimisations and speed.

- `pl.sql("SELECT ... FROM df")` finds DataFrames and LazyFrames by their Python variable names in the surrounding code and returns a LazyFrame (pass `eager=True` for a DataFrame).
- `df.sql("SELECT ... FROM self")` queries one table, which is called `self`.
- `pl.SQLContext(orders=lf1, users=lf2)` registers tables under names you choose, and `ctx.execute(query)` runs a query. Prefer it in real applications, where finding tables by variable name is too surprising.

Supported SQL covers `SELECT`, `WHERE` (filter), `GROUP BY` and `HAVING` (filter after grouping), `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT`, joins, `UNION` (stack results), `WITH` (name a sub-query to reuse), window functions with `OVER`, `CASE` (like when/then), and many text, maths and date functions. Files can be tables too: `SELECT ... FROM read_parquet('file.parquet')`.

In Polars 2, checking is postponed: mistakes in the SQL, or unknown tables and columns, only show up when you collect or call `collect_schema()`, not when you call `sql()`. Also, decimal numbers written in the query, like `1.5`, become exact `Decimal` values rather than floats.

SQL and expressions mix freely: run a SQL query, then keep chaining `.with_columns(...)` on the LazyFrame it returns.
concepts.code:
import polars as pl

orders = pl.DataFrame({"uid": [1, 1, 2, 3], "total": [10, 5, 7, 9]})
users = pl.DataFrame({"uid": [1, 2, 3], "country": ["NO", "SE", "NO"]})

ctx = pl.SQLContext(orders=orders, users=users)
q = ctx.execute("""
    SELECT u.country, SUM(o.total) AS revenue, COUNT(*) AS n
    FROM orders o JOIN users u ON o.uid = u.uid
    GROUP BY u.country
    ORDER BY revenue DESC
""")
print(type(q).__name__)                     # LazyFrame
out = q.with_columns(avg=pl.col("revenue") / pl.col("n")).collect()
print(out.rows())   # [('NO', 24, 3, 8.0), ('SE', 7, 1, 7.0)]
takeaways: SQL is translated into the same optimised lazy plans as expressions
Use `SQLContext` with explicit table names in real code
Mistakes surface only when you collect, in Polars 2
pitfalls: Expecting `pl.sql` to check column names immediately: in Polars 2 it fails only when collected.

quiz.q: What does SQLContext.execute(query) return by default?
options: A LazyFrame you can keep chaining or collect
quiz.explain: Queries are lazy by default; pass eager=True to get a DataFrame.

concepts.name: Streaming and larger-than-memory data
concepts.summary: Process data bigger than RAM with the streaming engine, sink_* outputs, results in pieces and hive-partitioned folders.
concepts.why: When data outgrows memory, streaming lets one computer do work that would otherwise need a group of machines.
concepts.body:
The **streaming engine**, the default for `collect()` in Polars 2, cuts the data into small pieces of rows (Polars calls them morsels) and pushes each through the plan on all cores. Steps like filter, select and with_columns handle one piece at a time without remembering anything. Group-bys, joins and sorts must remember state across pieces; when that state grows too large they split the work and spill some of it to disk. So most queries need far less memory than the size of their input.

To avoid ever holding the result in memory, write it straight to a file with a **sink**: `lf.sink_parquet("out.parquet")`, `sink_csv`, `sink_ipc` (Arrow's own file format), `sink_ndjson`. Sinks can also split the output into folders by a column's value, e.g. `pl.PartitionBy("out/", key="country")`. To handle results piece by piece in Python, loop over `lf.collect_batches()`.

Inputs scale the same way. Big data sets are often stored with **hive partitioning**: folders named after column values, like `year=2026/month=03/`. `pl.scan_parquet("data/**/*.parquet", hive_partitioning=True)` reads such a folder tree and turns the folder names into columns, so a filter on `year` skips whole folders. Files in cloud storage (`s3://`, `gs://`, `az://` addresses for Amazon, Google and Microsoft storage) work too, with login details passed in `storage_options`.

Things that defeat streaming: Python UDFs that need the whole column at once, steps that need the order of the entire data (some `over` and `rolling` patterns), and calling `collect()` on a result that is itself huge. Check the plan with `lf.explain()`, and keep memory flat by finishing with a sink.

Tune with `pl.Config.set_streaming_chunk_size` only after measuring; the defaults are usually right.
concepts.code:
import os
import polars as pl

os.makedirs("raw", exist_ok=True)
for i in range(3):   # pretend these are huge files
    pl.DataFrame({"country": ["NO", "SE"] * 2, "amount": [i, i + 1, i + 2, i + 3]}) \
      .write_parquet(f"raw/part{i}.parquet")

q = (
    pl.scan_parquet("raw/*.parquet")
    .filter(pl.col("amount") > 1)
    .group_by("country")
    .agg(total=pl.col("amount").sum())
)
q.sink_parquet("totals.parquet")        # result written straight to disk
print(pl.read_parquet("totals.parquet").sort("country").rows())
# [('NO', 11), ('SE', 17)]

for batch in pl.scan_parquet("raw/*.parquet").collect_batches():
    print(batch.height, end=" ")        # pieces arrive one by one, e.g. 4 4 4
takeaways: Polars 2 collects with the streaming engine: in pieces, on all cores, with limited memory
Finish with `sink_*` so the result never has to fit in RAM
Hive-partitioned scans skip whole folders when you filter on the folder columns
pitfalls: Streaming a huge query and then calling `collect()` on a result that is itself too large for memory.

quiz.q: Why end a large query with sink_parquet instead of collect().write_parquet()?
options: The result is written piece by piece and never fully held in memory
quiz.explain: A sink writes output to disk as it is produced, so memory use stays limited even when the result is large.

concepts.name: Python UDFs vs native code and plugins
concepts.summary: Know the cost of map_elements and map_batches, how to stay with built-in expressions, and when to write a Rust plugin.
concepts.why: One careless Python lambda can make a Polars query 10 to 100 times slower; experts know when to avoid UDFs and what to use instead.
concepts.body:
Polars runs expressions in compiled Rust code over Arrow memory, on many threads at once. Python code breaks that model, because the standard Python interpreter has the **GIL** (global interpreter lock): only one thread can run Python code at a time.

- **`map_elements(f, return_dtype=...)`** calls a Python function once per value. It holds the GIL, so it runs on one thread; it turns every value into a Python object; and the optimiser can't see inside it. It is the last resort. Polars even warns when it recognises a lambda it could translate into a built-in expression.
- **`map_batches(f)`** calls the function once per whole Series (or per piece of one), so a function built from NumPy whole-array operations stays fast. NumPy ufuncs can be applied directly: `np.log(pl.col("x"))` is handled without leaving the engine. If a column is stored in several chunks, the function may be called once per chunk, so it must give the same answer either way.
- **`pl.struct(...).map_batches`** passes several columns at once.

Before writing a UDF, look for a built-in way: the `str`, `list`, `dt` and `struct` methods, `pl.when`, `list.eval`, `fold`/`reduce` across columns, or `replace` and `replace_strict` for mapping values to other values.

When you truly need custom logic at full speed, write an **expression plugin**: a Rust function compiled with the `pyo3-polars` tools and registered with `polars.plugins.register_plugin_function`. Plugins run on all cores without the GIL and appear in query plans like built-in expressions. And always set `return_dtype` on Python UDFs, so a lazy query knows its result types without running.
concepts.code:
import time
import numpy as np
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"x": np.arange(1, 1_000_001, dtype=np.float64)})

t = time.perf_counter()
slow = df.select(pl.col("x").map_elements(lambda v: v * 2 + 1,
                                          return_dtype=pl.Float64))
t_slow = time.perf_counter() - t

t = time.perf_counter()
fast = df.select(pl.col("x") * 2 + 1)          # native expression
t_fast = time.perf_counter() - t

batch = df.select(pl.col("x").map_batches(np.log, return_dtype=pl.Float64))
print(slow.equals(fast), round(batch["x"][0], 3))   # True 0.0
print(f"native ~{t_slow / t_fast:.0f}x faster")     # often 10-100x, machine-dependent
takeaways: `map_elements` = Python per value: slow, one thread, invisible to the optimiser
`map_batches` with NumPy whole-array code is acceptable
Rust expression plugins give custom logic at built-in speed
pitfalls: Using `map_elements` for logic that a built-in method, `when/then` or `replace` already covers.

quiz.q: Why does a map_elements lambda block predicate pushdown?
options: The optimiser can't see inside Python code, so it can't move filters past it
quiz.explain: UDFs are black boxes to the optimiser, so it must assume they depend on every row.

concepts.name: Arrow memory, chunks and interop
concepts.summary: Understand Polars' Arrow-based columns, chunks and rechunk, string storage, categoricals, and zero-copy exchange with other libraries.
concepts.why: Memory layout explains Polars' speed, the cost of converting to other libraries, and many surprises around copies and types.
concepts.body:
Each Polars Series is stored as a list of **chunks**: separate blocks of Arrow memory. Each chunk holds a run of values plus a validity bitmap, one bit per row saying whether the value is null. Stacking tables or reading many files just adds chunks instead of copying data. Many chunks slow some operations down, so `df.rechunk()` merges them into one continuous block; `df.n_chunks()` shows how many there are.

Text uses Arrow's string-view layout. Each string gets a 16-byte entry: short strings fit inside it, and longer ones point into shared memory. That makes taking parts of text, filtering and joining cheap. For text with few distinct values repeated many times, use `pl.Categorical` (each distinct string stored once, plus a small whole number per row) or `pl.Enum([...])` when the allowed values are fixed and known. Both save memory and speed up group-bys and joins. In Polars 2, categoricals always sort alphabetically.

Exchange with other libraries follows the Arrow layout:

- `df.to_arrow()` and `pl.from_arrow(table)` (for the PyArrow library) are usually **zero-copy**: they share memory instead of copying it.
- `s.to_numpy()` is zero-copy for a number column with no nulls in a single chunk; otherwise it copies (nulls become NaN in decimal columns).
- `df.to_pandas()` copies by default; `use_pyarrow_extension_array=True` keeps Arrow-backed columns.
- Polars supports the Arrow PyCapsule interface (the `__arrow_c_stream__` method), a standard way for Python libraries such as DuckDB and PyArrow to hand over Arrow data without copying. The older DataFrame interchange protocol was removed in Polars 2.

`df.estimated_size("mb")` reports memory use, so you can check the effect of types and rechunking.
concepts.code:
import polars as pl
import pyarrow as pa

a = pl.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3]})
b = pl.DataFrame({"x": [4, 5]})
df = pl.concat([a, b], rechunk=False)
print(df.n_chunks())                    # 2  (no copy was made)
print(df.rechunk().n_chunks())          # 1

labels = pl.Series("city", ["Oslo, Norway (capital)", "Lima, Peru (capital)"] * 150_000)
enum = pl.Enum(["Lima, Peru (capital)", "Oslo, Norway (capital)"])
print([round(labels.cast(t).estimated_size("kb")) for t in (pl.String, pl.Categorical, enum)])
# [6152, 1172, 293]  (codes + one dictionary beat repeated strings)

tbl = df.rechunk().to_arrow()           # zero-copy Arrow table
print(isinstance(tbl, pa.Table), tbl.num_rows)   # True 5
arr = df.rechunk()["x"].to_numpy()      # zero-copy: numeric, no nulls, 1 chunk
print(arr.flags.writeable)              # False  (it views Polars' memory)
takeaways: A Series is a list of Arrow chunks; `rechunk()` merges them into one block
Categorical and Enum shrink repeated text
Arrow and PyCapsule exchange is zero-copy; pandas conversion usually copies
pitfalls: Writing to a NumPy array obtained from `to_numpy()` and expecting it to be a private copy.

quiz.q: When is Series.to_numpy() zero-copy?
options: For number data without nulls stored in a single chunk
quiz.explain: NumPy needs one continuous block of numbers with no null markers, so data in several chunks or with nulls must be copied.
